title: [recoverability] Every engine is refused a URL with a password, the wholesale environment prints, process listings with arguments and Claude Code's settings by any path, and its task says what to do instead (the accidental prints of url-leak-sources.md)
prompt:
Read CREDENTIAL_DENY and claude_settings in crates/spawn-core/src/bridge.rs (the deny list every engine gets in its --settings), and CREDENTIALS_LINE in crates/spawn-cli/src/deliver.rs (the line every task's prompt carries).

The record (rev-b, sync/url-leak-sources.md). A database URL with its password reached 16 transcripts. Every time it came through an agent's own Bash command, between 2026-11-06 and 11-08:
- (1) An agent read a credential file.
- (2)+(3) An agent wrote the literal URL into its command line. It then showed in other agents' `ps -o args` and `pgrep -af` output.
- (5) An agent printed its environment (`env | grep …`). Claude Code also hands every tool shell the env block of ~/.claude/settings.json, which holds the gateway key (lead-mac, 11-13), so a wholesale print shows that key too.
Engines' environments still hold SPAWN_TEST_DATABASE_URL, and the supervisor's also holds SPAWN_DATABASE_URL. CREDENTIAL_DENY refuses the credential files by name, `*/environ*` and `ps …e`. It does not refuse the wholesale prints, process listings with arguments, a URL on a command line, or `cd ~/.claude && grep … settings.json`.
This objective closes the accidental shell prints. It does not refuse `echo $X`, `env -u X` with no command (a glob cannot tell it from `env -u X cmd`), or a python or node one-liner that prints the environment: engines' environments that hold no password (objectives A1 and A2, next) close the source. A deny list matches text, so a reader that builds a path from pieces gets past it; that is also A1/A2's to close.

Required behaviour. CREDENTIAL_DENY gains these 141 entries, exactly (rsi/scenarios/108.sh lists them):
- `Bash(*://*:*@*)`: a URL that holds a password anywhere in a command.
- For each of `env`, `printenv`, `export -p`, `declare -x`, `set`, `export`, `declare`, `declare -p`, `typeset`, `typeset -p`, `typeset -x`, `env -0`, `env --null`, `/usr/bin/env` and `command env` (P): `Bash(P)`, `Bash(P |*)`, `Bash(P|*)`, `Bash(*; P)`, `Bash(*&& P)`, `Bash(*; P |*)` and `Bash(*&& P |*)`. That is the print alone, or behind a pipe, `;` or `&&`, so that the refusal does not depend on Claude Code splitting the command.
- The process listings with arguments (source 3): `Bash(*ps -ef*)`, `Bash(*ps -fe*)`, `Bash(*ps -eF*)`, `Bash(*ps -f *)`, `Bash(*ps -fp*)`, `Bash(*ps aux*)`, `Bash(*ps axu*)`, `Bash(*ps -aux*)`, `Bash(*ps *args*)`, `Bash(*ps *cmd*)`, `Bash(*ps *command*)`, `Bash(*pgrep* -a*)`, `Bash(*pgrep* -fa*)`, `Bash(*pgrep* -af*)`, `Bash(*pgrep* -l*)`, `Bash(*pgrep* -fl*)`, `Bash(*pgrep* -lf*)`, `Bash(*pgrep* --list*)`, `Bash(*ps ax*)`, `Bash(*ps x*)`, `Bash(*ps -e -f*)`, `Bash(*ps -A -f*)`, `Bash(*ps -Af*)`, `Bash(*ps -wwf*)`, `Bash(*ps -wf*)`, `Bash(*top *-c*)`, `Bash(*pstree -a*)`, `Bash(*pstree -pa*)`, `Bash(*pstree -ap*)`, `Bash(*pstree * -a*)`, `Bash(*/cmdline*)` and `Read(//proc/**)`.
- Claude Code's settings by any path (source 1, the gateway key): `Bash(*/.claude*)`, `Bash(*cd .claude*)` and `Bash(*settings.local.json*)`.
The credential files read by any reader (head, tail, less, more, grep, sed, awk, xxd, od, base64, strings, cp/dd, a python/perl/node one-liner): the existing rules refuse any Bash command whose text names the file (`*spawn.env*` covers spawn.env.bak-relay and .bak-webdir, `*.config/spawn*`, `*test-database.url*`, …), and `Read(...)` covers Claude Code's file tools. The scenario proves that for each reader on its whole text. The entries above add the forms that got past them.
Every engine gets the list, as today.
- A deny rule carries no message of its own (Claude Code's denial names the rule), and the Bridge reads engines only from transcript and screen: no hooks. So CREDENTIALS_LINE says what to do instead, appended to today's text: "A command that prints the whole environment, lists processes with their arguments, reads a credential file or holds a URL with its password is refused: the variable is already in your environment; name it ($SPAWN_TEST_DATABASE_URL), never expand or print it; find a process with `pgrep -f` (pids only) or `ps -p <pid>`, in a command of its own."
- These still run: `env VAR=x cmd`, `env -u` / `env -i …` with a command, `printenv HOME`, `set -e` / `set -euo pipefail`, `export FOO=bar`, `declare -a`, a URL without a password (`postgres://u@host/db`, `http://127.0.0.1:8787/…`), `ps -p <pid>`, `ps -o pid,etime -p <pid>`, `pgrep -f`/`-x` (pids only), `kill <pid>`, `cat /proc/loadavg`, `ls ~/.config`, `declare -p FOO`, `top -b -n 1`, `pstree -p`, `ps -p 1 -o pid,etime`.

False refusals that were thought of and accepted, all rare:
- A command whose text holds `user:pass@` after `://` for another reason: a made-up URL in a heredoc or a `sed` that writes a fixture. Write such files with the editor tools, not Bash.
- A URL with a port and an `@` later in it (`curl 'http://h:8787/x?a=b@c'`).
- `*pgrep* -l*` and `*pgrep* -a*` match past pgrep's own words: `pgrep -f x && ls -la` is refused. Run the two apart.
- `*ps *args*`, `*ps *cmd*` and `*ps -f *` match any word ending in "ps" followed later by those letters (`ls caps cmd.txt`).
- `*/.claude*`, `*cd .claude*` and `*settings.local.json*` refuse a workspace's own .claude directory too.
What an agent will meet, and what the line tells it to do instead, so that a refusal does not cost a turn of guessing:
- `pgrep -f x && ls -la` is refused: find the process in a command of its own (`pgrep -f x`, pids only, or `ps -p <pid>`).
- `env | grep PG`, `printenv | grep DATABASE`: name the variable ($SPAWN_TEST_DATABASE_URL) in the command that needs it; never print it.
- `psql 'postgres://u:pw@…'`: use the variable, not its value.
- a fixture with a made-up `user:pass@` URL written through a Bash heredoc: write it with the editor tools.
Not covered on the whole text, but by Claude Code's splitting: a print on a new line of a multi-line command, and `||`.

Of lead-mac's 09:08 additions, 108 takes all of them: the credential files read by any reader (head, tail, less, more, grep, sed, awk, xxd, od, base64, strings, cp, dd, python/perl/node), and the process listings with arguments (ps -ef, ps aux, ps -o args/cmd, pgrep -a/-l, /proc/<pid>/cmdline and environ). Left to a follow-up: none of those. What a deny list cannot stop (a path or a command built from pieces, `echo $X`, a one-liner that prints the environment) is A1/A2's to close, at the source.

Files (expected; no other open objective touches them): crates/spawn-core/src/bridge.rs (CREDENTIAL_DENY and its unit test) and crates/spawn-cli/src/deliver.rs (CREDENTIALS_LINE and its test). About 100 lines.

Acceptance: rsi/scenarios/108.sh. A real `spawn loop` runs a mission with an objective backlog and a resident on a fake engine, which keeps the --settings it is handed and every line typed into it. One objective is assigned and delivered (to the resident, which takes objective work).
(1) The deny list handed to every engine started holds each of the 141 entries exactly. An edit that drops one fails.
(2) Matched as Claude Code documents its Bash rules (`*` matches any text; a compound command is also checked one part at a time), the list refuses each of 72 commands on its whole text (among them the forms agents used in the record: env | grep, env | sort, printenv | grep, set | grep, export -p, cat /proc/self/environ, tr '\0' '\n' < /proc/<pid>/environ), and none of 27 others, neither whole nor in any part. The commands are text: none is run, no real value is used, and no credential file is read.
(3) The task typed into the engine carries the sentence above.
The limit of the check: it cannot run Claude Code (no print mode), so it reads the list the Bridge hands a fake engine and matches it as Claude Code documents. It does not watch a real engine refuse a command.
check-tests.sh and check-clippy.sh must pass, and 106 (the same harness) must keep passing.
